summary: Mercaptopurine (6-MP) is a purine-analog antimetabolite indicated for maintenance treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia as part of combination chemotherapy. Usual dose is 1.5-2.5 mg/kg (50-75 mg/m2) once daily, titrated to neutrophil count. Myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity are the key dose-limiting toxicities; patients with TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency and those on allopurinol need substantial dose reduction.
indications: Treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) as part of a combination chemotherapy maintenance regimen

dosage.n: Adjust to maintain target ANC and for myelosuppression

dosage.d: Reduce mercaptopurine dose to about 25-33% of usual
Substantially reduce dose (homozygous-deficient may need large reductions)
dosage.n: Test in severe or repeated myelosuppression

admin: Take orally once daily, consistently either with or without food
Take consistently apart from milk/dairy products which may reduce absorption

moa: Mercaptopurine is a purine analog that is transported into cells and converted to thioguanine nucleotides (TGNs). Incorporation of TGNs into DNA and RNA causes cell-cycle arrest and cell death, and the metabolites also inhibit de novo purine synthesis and purine nucleotide interconversion, producing cytotoxicity in proliferating leukemic cells.

absolute: Prior resistance to mercaptopurine or thioguanine (cross-resistance)

preg: Mercaptopurine can cause fetal harm; first-trimester exposure increases miscarriage and it was embryolethal/teratogenic in animals. Advise patients of reproductive potential to use effective contraception and avoid pregnancy during treatment.
lact: Advise patients not to breastfeed during treatment with mercaptopurine and for a period after the final dose, due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in the infant.
renal: Use the lowest recommended starting dose, or increase the dosing interval, in renal impairment because mercaptopurine and its metabolites are renally cleared and accumulation increases toxicity.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity (intrahepatic cholestasis, hepatic necrosis) can occur. Use the lowest recommended starting dose in hepatic impairment, monitor transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, and withhold the drug at the onset of hepatotoxicity.

major: Allopurinol - inhibits xanthine oxidase, raising mercaptopurine levels; reduce 6-MP dose to ~25-33%
Other myelosuppressive drugs - additive bone marrow suppression
moderate: Warfarin - mercaptopurine may reduce anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Aminosalicylates (mesalamine, sulfasalazine, olsalazine) - inhibit TPMT, raising toxicity
minor: Live vaccines - risk of disseminated infection in immunosuppressed patients
interactions.food: Take consistently with or without food; avoid taking with milk/dairy as xanthine oxidase in milk may degrade the drug.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol because of additive hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: May lower blood counts and raise transaminases, bilirubin and uric acid; reduces vaccine response.

rare: Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma and other secondary malignancies

monitoring: Complete blood count frequently; adjust dose for excessive myelosuppression
Liver function tests (transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin)
TPMT and NUDT15 status in severe or repeated myelosuppression
Bone marrow assessment if prolonged or repeated cytopenias
Signs of infection and of hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma
counsel: Take once daily at the same time, consistently with or without food (not with milk)
Avoid pregnancy and use reliable contraception; do not breastfeed
Report fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding immediately (low blood counts)
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine or right-sided abdominal pain (liver)
Tell your doctor about allopurinol or aminosalicylate use, which require dose changes
pk: Cytotoxic effect develops over days as TGNs accumulate
Plasma peak about 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Parent drug short (~1-2 h); active metabolites persist intracellularly
Once-daily dosing due to long-lived intracellular metabolites
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light
pearls: Test TPMT/NUDT15 in patients with severe or recurrent myelosuppression - deficient patients need large dose reductions
With allopurinol, cut the mercaptopurine dose to roughly one-quarter to one-third
Titrate to absolute neutrophil count, not a fixed dose
Aminosalicylates (mesalamine/sulfasalazine) inhibit TPMT and raise toxicity
Monitor LFTs - withhold at the onset of hepatotoxicity
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, then skip it - do not take a double dose. Tell your care team about missed doses, as dosing is titrated to blood counts.
overdose: Overdose may cause immediate gastrointestinal effects (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) or delayed myelosuppression, liver dysfunction and gastroenteritis. There is no antidote; dialysis is of marginal value because of rapid intracellular metabolism. Withhold the drug, give supportive care, and consider emesis if seen immediately after ingestion.
